# SGD and Stochastic Approximation

Stochastic gradient descent is a fundamentally different algorithm from batch GD, with its own convergence theory (Robbins-Monro), regularisation properties, and systems engineering requirements.

## SGD as Noisy Gradient Descent

ĝ_B = (1/B)Σᵢ∈B ∇Lᵢ(θ): unbiased (E[ĝ_B] = ∇L) with variance σ²/B. Iterates form a Markov chain fluctuating around the minimum with radius ∝ η·σ/√B.

## Robbins-Monro Conditions

Σₜ ηₜ = ∞ (sufficient exploration) and Σₜ ηₜ² < ∞ (bounded variance accumulation) → convergence. Classic: ηₜ = η₀/t. Modern LLM training: warmup + cosine (violates RM but works empirically).

## Implicit Regularisation

SGD noise biases toward flat (wide) minima. Larger batch size → less noise → sharper minima → worse generalisation. This is why effective batch size must be balanced against generalisation quality.

## Data Shuffling

Shuffle the full dataset each epoch before drawing minibatches. Without shuffling, gradient estimates are biased toward recent data distribution.

## Gradient Accumulation

```python
for i, (x, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
    loss = model(x, y) / accum_steps
    loss.backward()
    if (i + 1) % accum_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step(); optimizer.zero_grad()
```

Achieves effective batch B_eff = accum_steps × batch_size without extra VRAM.

## The Linear Scaling Rule

LR ∝ B: multiply LR by k when batch size multiplied by k (Goyal et al. 2017). Breaks for very large k. Square-root scaling (η ∝ √B) is theoretically justified in the noise-dominated regime.

## Distributed SGD

AllReduce averages gradients across R workers: Ring-AllReduce in O(2N(R−1)/R) communication. Gradient compression (PowerSGD, 1-bit SGD) reduces bandwidth. ZeRO shards optimizer states.
